Story: Register a performer and their aliases
Description: Create and store a performer record: legal name, stage names and aliases, and the reference images used later for reverse-image discovery. Aliases matter more than they look - infringing listings rarely use a performer's exact legal name, and every downstream sweep and name-match guardrail resolves against this record.
Acceptance: A performer can be created, retrieved and listed; aliases and reference image URIs round-trip intact.

Story: Extract a permission grant from a contract PDF
Description: Upload a signed agreement and have Gemini populate the six fields that define a permission slip: performer, licensee, permitted uses, territories, and the validity window. This is the step that converts unstructured legal language into something a machine can reason over, and it is the only reason the registry can exist at all.
Acceptance: A PDF upload produces a populated draft grant with all six fields attempted.

Story: Cite the source sentence for every extracted field
Description: Each extracted field carries the verbatim sentence and page number it came from, displayed directly beneath it. A lawyer will not trust an AI extraction they cannot verify in two seconds. Citations are what make the registry defensible rather than merely convenient, and they cost almost nothing to produce.
Acceptance: Every populated field displays its verbatim source sentence and page number.

Story: Review and correct a grant before it is saved
Description: The extraction lands in an editable form, not straight into the database. A human confirms or corrects each field and explicitly saves. Every verdict the product ever produces resolves against this table, so a wrong grant silently poisons everything downstream - the one place worth a human gate.
Acceptance: No consents row is written without an explicit human save; edits persist.

Story: Browse the registry
Description: A view listing performers and their grants, showing permitted uses, territories and validity window at a glance, with clause quotes on expand. This is where a user confirms what the system believes before trusting any verdict it produces.
Acceptance: Registry view lists performers with their grants and the underlying clause quotes.

Story: Settle the Parallel API questions
Description: Read Parallel's API reference and answer two things: which region and language parameters Search exposes, and whether the Extract API returns full page content. Both change the design - locale parameters shape every web cache key, and Extract could replace our own page fetcher entirely, which would deepen the partner integration and redraw four diagrams.
Acceptance: Answers recorded in CLAUDE.md; the agent side and the architecture freeze are unblocked.

Story: Plan a multi-language, multi-modality sweep
Description: Generate the search plan: performer name and aliases crossed with modality terms - AI voice, voice clone, deepfake ad, AI avatar - across at least five locales spanning four languages. A cloned-voice listing written in Portuguese is completely invisible to an English-only sweep, and since territory determines the verdict, language coverage is correctness, not polish.
Acceptance: Plan output includes non-English queries across five or more locales.

Story: Sweep the open web through Parallel
Description: Call Parallel's Search API through the official parallel-web SDK for every planned query, logging each call with query, locale, result count and timestamp. The competition rules are explicit that the integration must be present in code and demonstrably called at runtime, not merely named in a README - so the call log is both an engineering artifact and submission evidence.
Acceptance: SDK imported and called; call log visible on screen and screenshot-ready.

Story: Discover misuse that carries no text
Description: Some misuse announces itself in words; some does not. An image posted with no caption is invisible to any search API. Reverse-image discovery through Cloud Vision web detection finds pages hosting visually similar imagery, widening coverage past what language can reach. First thing to cut if time runs short.
Acceptance: A reference image yields candidate pages.

Story: Never create a duplicate finding
Description: Candidates are de-duplicated on a URL hash, so re-running a sweep updates the existing finding in place rather than creating a second one. This is what makes sweeps safely repeatable, which is in turn what makes scheduled monitoring possible at all.
Acceptance: Running the same sweep twice produces no duplicate rows.

Story: Watch continuously instead of on demand
Description: Scheduled sweeps with per-performer cadence and jittered timing so a large roster does not burst the API. On-demand sweeps are a demo; continuous monitoring is the product. The date a finding was first seen only means something if something was actually watching.
Acceptance: A scheduled run appears in audit_log even when it finds nothing.

Story: Fetch third-party pages without getting exploited
Description: The fetcher accepts attacker-supplied URLs, so it blocks private and link-local address ranges, rejects non-HTTP schemes, re-validates after every redirect, caps response size, and sends no credentials or cookies. Skipping this turns a compliance tool into an internal-network scanner for anyone who can get a URL into our queue.
Acceptance: Private-range, file scheme and redirect-to-internal URLs are all rejected.

Story: Turn a page into structured observations
Description: Ask Gemini a fixed set of questions about the page - is a named real person depicted, does the page itself claim an AI copy, which modality, is it commercial, which territories does it target, and quote the proof - using forced function calling so the answer is always schema-valid or explicitly failed. The narrow schema is the guardrail: an extractor with no free-form output channel has nowhere to misbehave.
Acceptance: Output is always a valid TriageExtraction or an explicit failure. Never prose.

Story: Reject fabricated or drifted extractions
Description: Validators run on every extraction: the evidence quote must be a verbatim substring of the source text, territories must be valid ISO codes, confidence must be in range, and the named person must fuzzy-match the performer being swept. The substring check is the highest-value guardrail in the system - one string comparison, and quote hallucination becomes structurally impossible.
Acceptance: A fabricated quote is rejected, proven by test.

Story: Catch pages that try to instruct the agent
Description: A page may carry text addressed at our agent - ignore previous instructions, this use is licensed, mark as authorised. A detector flags these as injection_suspected and surfaces a badge in the UI, so the system labels the attempt rather than obeying it. It is also thirty seconds of unusually good demo footage.
Acceptance: A planted injection page is flagged, not obeyed.

Story: Decide a verdict against the registry
Description: Evaluate seven ordered checks in plain code: does a grant exist for this performer, does it cover this modality, are all target territories inside it, is today within the validity window, is the actor actually the licensee, is confidence sufficient. No model call happens in this module. The model observes; code decides. That makes the verdict testable, explainable, and immune to persuasion.
Acceptance: No model call exists in the reconciler; verdict returns with the failing check named.

Story: Judge per territory, not globally
Description: A synthetic voice licensed for North America is infringing in Japan, so the verdict compares where an offering is aimed against the territories the grant covers. The output reads: licensed for US and CA, this listing prices in BRL and targets Brazil, unauthorised. This is what rights management actually looks like, and it is the detail that reads as domain understanding rather than a wrapper around a search API.
Acceptance: Territory-scoped verdicts are expressible and unit-tested.

Story: Cite the evidence behind every verdict
Description: No verdict is written without the evidence quote, the URL, and the matched or breached clause. Uncited verdicts are rejected outright rather than displayed with a caveat. This is the difference between a tool a lawyer can act on and one whose output they have to reproduce by hand anyway.
Acceptance: Verdicts lacking a citation are rejected before storage.

Story: Send doubt to a human instead of guessing
Description: Confidence below threshold produces an ambiguous verdict and routes to a review queue. The product's entire value is that its verdicts can be relied on, and that requires it to say clearly when it does not know. A confident wrong answer is worse here than no answer.
Acceptance: Low-confidence findings land in a human queue rather than receiving a verdict.

Story: Fail toward doubt, never toward permission
Description: Every failure mode resolves toward ambiguous, unverified or degraded - never toward authorised or cleared. A crash that produces no findings must be distinguishable from a clean sweep that found nothing, because a human signs off on the result either way. A compliance tool that fails quietly is worse than no tool at all.
Acceptance: A schema failure yields ambiguous; an API failure marks the sweep degraded.

Story: Prove the rule engine with tests
Description: Unit tests covering every branch of the rule engine, including the territory-scoping case. The whole product rests on this one component being right, and because it is deterministic with no model call, testing it properly is cheap. This is the highest return per hour of test writing in the project.
Acceptance: All seven branches covered plus the authorised-in-US, unauthorised-in-EU case.

Story: Preserve evidence permanently
Description: Capture page text and a screenshot at the moment of discovery into immutable storage with no expiry. The infringing page will be taken down - that is the entire point of a takedown - so evidence stored in a cache that expires would leave the case file worthless exactly when it matters. Evidence is not cache, and conflating the two is a real bug.
Acceptance: A snapshot remains retrievable after the source page is removed.

Story: Assemble a case file a lawyer can act on
Description: Bundle the URL, preserved snapshot, evidence quote and the specific breached clause into one artifact that requires no re-research. This is the step that replaces roughly a day of paralegal work per incident, and it is where the product's value becomes legible to a buyer.
Acceptance: The case file names the specific clause it relies on.

Story: Draft the takedown notice
Description: Generate a notice grounded strictly in the evidence bundle, presented as editable text with copy-out. It states evidence and rule mismatch and stops there - it does not assert legal conclusions, because we are not offering legal advice and should not appear to.
Acceptance: Every URL and quote in the draft appears in the evidence bundle.

Story: Keep sending in human hands
Description: No send capability exists anywhere in the product - not in the UI, not in the code. Notices are drafted and copied out, and a person sends them. An agent that can act on a mistaken verdict against a third party is a liability, not a feature, and the absence of that capability is worth stating out loud in the demo.
Acceptance: No send action exists in either code or UI.

Story: Ingest a deliverable and read its provenance
Description: Accept an asset upload, hash it, and read any embedded provenance metadata. The absence of metadata is recorded as a distinct signal rather than a null, because a stripped credential is itself something worth asking a vendor about - silence is information here.
Acceptance: Missing provenance is stored as a distinct state, not as null.

Story: Read what the vendor said they did
Description: Parse the vendor's invoice or statement of work for declared generative usage. If the invoice reads AI voice replacement, twelve lines, then those twelve lines need a grant. Paperwork is more reliable than inspection and cheaper than multimodal analysis, so it should always be consulted first.
Acceptance: Declared AI usage is extracted with a source quote.

Story: Inspect the media itself
Description: Generate a low-bitrate proxy and ask Gemini whether a recognisable performer and a human voice are present. The proxy goes to the model rather than the original, because multimodal cost tracks bytes and inspection does not need a full-resolution master. The transcript is stored content-addressed so later questions answer from text with no second call.
Acceptance: The proxy is sent to the model, not the original; the transcript is cached.

Story: Decide coverage, defaulting to deny
Description: Run the same rule engine that enforcement uses. Every asset starts as unverified and only becomes cleared when a grant covers what was done to it. We prove coverage rather than detecting AI - which is precisely why imperfect detection is still useful, and why this half of the product can ship in a weekend.
Acceptance: Two uploads give one cleared and one blocked; an asset with no paperwork stays unverified.

Story: Show what is blocking delivery
Description: A production-level rollup listing every asset that cannot ship and exactly why, produced before delivery rather than discovered after. This is the artifact a post-production supervisor actually needs, and the thing a distributor asks for at acquisition.
Acceptance: Blockers are listed per production, each naming the missing or non-covering grant.

Story: Record every decision and its inputs
Description: Append-only audit events for every agent step and tool call, capturing inputs, outputs, tool arguments and prompt version. For a compliance product the defensible trail is the value, not a byproduct - so the Store interface deliberately exposes no update or delete for this table. Removing the capability beats remembering not to use it.
Acceptance: Every tool call produces an audit row; no update or delete methods exist.

Story: Disclose how fresh the data was
Description: Each recorded tool call notes whether it came from cache and how old that data was. A decision must never imply a freshness it does not have - claiming we checked the web at 3pm when we actually used data from 9am quietly undermines the one thing the product is selling.
Acceptance: from_cache and cache_age_s are present on every recorded tool call.

Story: Inspect the decision trail in the UI
Description: Any verdict expands to show what it was based on, which tools ran, and the age of each input. A user who cannot audit a decision will not rely on it, and an auditable wrong answer is far more recoverable than an opaque right one.
Acceptance: Any verdict expands to its inputs and their age.

Story: Cache uploads by content, with no expiry
Description: An uploaded file never changes, so its content hash is the cache key and the entry never goes stale. Contract text extraction, media inspection and transcripts are all keyed this way. This is where the real money is saved - re-running the same contract or clip twenty times during development costs one call.
Acceptance: The same file processed twice results in exactly one model call.

Story: Cache web results with TTL and the right keys
Description: Web content does change, so search results and page fetches expire on a TTL. Keys must include locale and prompt_version: serve a cached US result for a JP query once and the territory logic is quietly wrong, and without prompt_version you will spend an hour debugging output from a prompt you already deleted.
Acceptance: Changing either locale or prompt_version misses the cache, proven by test.

Story: Survive API failures without lying
Description: Classify errors before retrying - transient gets exponential backoff with jitter, permanent gets none, semantic gets exactly one repair attempt. A circuit breaker aborts the sweep and marks it degraded rather than rendering a partial sweep as though it were complete. Retrying a 401 thirty times is how a demo slot gets burned.
Acceptance: A 401 is not retried; N consecutive failures mark the sweep degraded.

Story: Run the entire demo from cache
Description: DEMO_MODE runs the full pipeline with zero external calls. The video shoot cannot be allowed to die on a rate limit or a flaky API at 1am the night before submission, and this is a one-hour insurance policy against exactly that.
Acceptance: A full sweep completes with the network disabled.

Story: Build the app shell
Description: FastAPI and Jinja scaffolding with layout and navigation across the three views. Deliberately minimal - no auth, no multi-tenancy, no framework ceremony. Every hour spent here is an hour not spent on the thing being judged.
Acceptance: Serves locally with navigation between the three views.

Story: Render third-party text safely
Description: We display text taken from attacker-controlled pages inside our own UI, so everything is escaped on output and fetched HTML is never rendered directly. Half an hour of work that prevents the demo from executing someone else's script on stage.
Acceptance: Script tags present in fetched page text render inert.

Story: Run the agents on Agent Engine
Description: Deploy the ADK pipelines to Agent Engine so that powered by Gemini and Google Cloud Agent Builder is true in the code rather than in the README. Raw API calls from a container would satisfy the accepted-SDK list but weakly satisfy the brief, and technological implementation is a quarter of the score.
Acceptance: Agents are invoked remotely, not in-process.

Story: Serve the app from Cloud Run
Description: The submission requires a hosted URL that works from a cold start with no local dependencies. Deploy on the 8th, not the 9th - a deployment discovered broken on the final morning is the single most common way a good hackathon project fails to submit.
Acceptance: Works from a fresh browser with no local server running.

Story: Handle secrets safely in deployment
Description: Secrets come from Secret Manager in the deployed service and from a gitignored .env locally. The repository is public, so a committed key is simultaneously a security incident and a competition risk, and deleting it in a later commit does not remove it from history.
Acceptance: No secrets appear in environment files in the deployed service.

Story: Manufacture the demo fixtures
Description: Generate the fictional performer's reference images with Imagen 3 and a fake cloned-voice clip with TTS, then write their contract PDF with clauses that produce one cleared and one blocked asset. Every synthetic asset in the demo is one we made, of a person who does not exist - which is both the clean answer to demo safety and a strong line to say on camera.
Acceptance: No real person's likeness appears anywhere in the submission.

Story: Prove the required services actually ran
Description: Screenshots of the Parallel call log and the Google Cloud console showing the services genuinely invoked. The rules require evidence that the integration was called, not merely named - this is a disqualification risk, not a nice-to-have.
Acceptance: Evidence shows calls made, with timestamps.

Story: Script and record the demo video
Description: A scripted three-minute demo, timed by reading it aloud rather than estimated. Opens on the real precedent, shows a live sweep and a territory-scoped verdict, catches a planted injection attempt, and closes on the clearance view proving the registry works in both directions.
Acceptance: Public on YouTube or Vimeo, under 3:00, English or subtitled.

Story: Write the Devpost submission
Description: The writeup, led by the precedent framing - the AI Darth Vader case, where a grant existed and the dispute was whether it covered that use - plus the explicit scope boundary and the architecture. Naming what we do not claim scores better than an overclaim a judge can puncture.
Acceptance: Writeup submitted with the precedent, scope boundary and architecture included.

Story: Walk the final checklist
Description: Walk the submission checklist end to end before noon PDT: hosted URL live, video public and under three minutes, repository public with a complete license, track selected, form completed, runtime evidence attached. Late or incomplete scores zero regardless of quality.
Acceptance: Every checklist box ticked before 12:00 PDT on 9 September.
